text:
maria: Trying to run nsys inside a k8s pod to get kernel timelines for the recent perf regression. I can start the app but nsys says `No CUDA devices found` and when I try to trace /sys I get permission denied on /sys/kernel/tracing/trace_marker. Anyone ran into this in-cluster?

ajay: You need device nodes and some extra privileges. Quick checklist: pod must get `nvidia.com/gpu` from the device plugin, the container runtime must be the nvidia runtime (or use nvidia-container-toolkit), and you need either `--privileged` or capabilities for ptrace/sys_admin to access tracing and perf. Also mount the driver libs if you run an older image.

maria: Here's what I tried:
```
kubectl run profiler -it --image=redwood/runtime-debug --limits="nvidia.com/gpu=1" --restart=Never -- /bin/bash
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o /tmp/profile ./server
# -> nsys: No CUDA devices found
# and when I try: echo 1 > /sys/kernel/tracing/trace_marker
# -> bash: /sys/kernel/tracing/trace_marker: Permission denied
```

infra-bot: Run `kubectl describe pod profiler` and `kubectl exec -it profiler -- ls -l /dev | grep nvidia` to confirm device nodes are present. Also check the node has nvidia-driver installed. Device plugin should create `/dev/nvidia0`, `/dev/nvidiactl`, `/dev/nvidia-uvm`.

leo: We had a similar issue last quarter. Two practical fixes we used: either run the pod with `securityContext: privileged: true` (fastest for debugging) or keep the pod unprivileged but add caps and host mounts: add capabilities SYS_PTRACE and SYS_ADMIN, hostPID: true, and mount `/sys/kernel/tracing` as readOnly hostPath. Example snippet: 
```yaml
securityContext:
  privileged: true # debugging only
# OR for minimal privs:
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    add: ["SYS_PTRACE", "SYS_ADMIN"]
hostPID: true
volumes:
- name: tracefs
  hostPath:
    path: /sys/kernel/tracing
    type: Directory
volumeMounts:
- mountPath: /sys/kernel/tracing
  name: tracefs
  readOnly: true
```
Note: you also need the node device plugin; set `resources.limits.nvidia.com/gpu: 1` on the container spec.

maria: Adding privileged to the pod made nsys start collecting, thanks. I ran a quick capture and see a ton of `memcpy`/`cudaMemcpyAsync` overlap and long kernel launches for `attention_kernel_fwd`. Timeline excerpt: 
```
[GPU timeline] 0ms - memcpy H2D 0.4ms | kernel attention_fwd 12.3ms | memcpy D2H 0.2ms
[GPU timeline] kernel aten::copy_ 8.7ms overlaps kernel attention_fwd
[CPU timeline] thread-1 copying KV cache 6ms per request
```
Looks like kernel selection fell back to a slow kernel and KV cache copying is on the hot path.

ajay: Two things to check: 1) kernel selection - verify the runtime picked the optimized kernel for the model's sequence length and dtype (FP16/INT8). If the kernel matcher didn't find a small-seqlen kernel, it can launch a generic slower kernel. Check logs for the selected kernel name. 2) KV cache: if the implementation copies KV cache from pinned GPU memory to pageable host memory each request, you'll see CPU-side copies. Make sure pinned (page-locked) host memory is used for async transfers and that streams overlap properly.

sophie: FYI we also hit permission issues with perfetto in-cluster — perfetto needs access to `/sys/kernel/tracing` and often `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`. For production we avoid privileged pods; instead we run the profiler on the node (ssh) or use a short-lived DaemonSet with limited host mounts and RBAC. Example DaemonSet approach: mount `/dev/nvidia*`, `/sys/kernel/tracing`, set `hostPID: true`, add caps, and schedule to specific node using nodeSelector.

maria: Reproduced again with more capture. Found two concrete regressions:
- Kernel selector was choosing a 32-bit accumulator kernel when it should have picked the 16-bit optimized path for our fp16 model after a recent kernel table change. That explains the 2x kernel time.
- Batching heuristic was using a max-batch=1 for small requests because latency SLOs were configured aggressively; small batches force more kernels launches and poorer kernel choice.

leo: For the kernel table bug, push a deterministic unit test that runs the matcher with the model config and asserts the chosen kernel identifier. For batching, add a counterfactual config in the console to test slightly relaxed latency SLO (allow 3ms extra) to see if batching grows to 2-4 and reduces per-token cost/time.

ajay: Other operational tips for k8s profiling:
- Use `runtimeClassName: nvidia` or configure `nvidia.com/gpu` properly so device nodes are injected.
- When running nsys inside container, ensure the container image has the matching CUDA driver libs (or bind mount `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` driver libs from host).
- If you cannot run privileged, do profiling on the node and use `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx -t 60 --output node-profile` while the pod runs.

maria: Thanks all — next steps:
1) leo to add matcher unit tests and open PR for kernel table fix.
2) sophie to prototype DaemonSet-based profiler with minimal caps/hostPath (non-privileged if possible).
3) I'll run bandwidth tests and validate pinned memory transfers; will paste perf counters.

infra-bot: Created task PERF-482: "In-cluster GPU profiling playbook (nsys/Perfetto, minimal privileges)" and linked this thread.

ajay: If anyone needs my debug pod yaml lmk, I have a ready-to-use one with `capabilities: [SYS_PTRACE, SYS_ADMIN]`, `hostPID: true`, and nodeSelector `kubernetes.io/role=gpu`.

maria: Posting the debug pod yaml from ajay worked; captured a full 60s profile and the hotspot is confirmed. Thanks! :tada:
